{{Short description|Equivalence relation}}
In mathematics, specifically [[group theory]], '''isoclinism''' is an [[equivalence relation]] on [[group (mathematics)|groups]] which generalizes [[isomorphism]]. Isoclinism was introduced by {{harvtxt|Hall|1940}} to help classify and understand [[p-group]]s, although it is applicable to all groups.  Isoclinism also has  consequences<!--ATLAS p. xxiii, §6.7¶3--> for the [[Schur multiplier]] and the associated aspects of [[character theory]], as described in {{harvtxt|Suzuki|1982|p=256}} and {{harvtxt|Conway|Curtis|Norton|Parker|1985|p=xxiii|loc=Ch. 6.7}}. The word "isoclinism" comes from the Greek ισοκλινης meaning equal slope. 

Some textbooks discussing isoclinism include {{harvtxt|Berkovich|2008|loc=§29}} and {{harvtxt|Blackburn|Neumann|Venkataraman|2007|loc=§21.2}} and {{harvtxt|Suzuki|1986|pp=92–95}}. 

==Definition==

The isoclinism class of a group ''G'' is determined by the groups ''G''/''Z''(''G'') (the [[inner automorphism|inner automorphism group]]) and ''{{prime|G}}'' (the  [[commutator subgroup]]) and the commutator map from ''G''/''Z''(''G'') × ''G''/''Z''(''G'') to ''{{prime|G}}'' (taking ''a'', ''b'' to ''aba<sup>−1</sup>b<sup>−1</sup>''). 

In other words,  two groups ''G''<sub>1</sub> and ''G''<sub>2</sub> are isoclinic if there are isomorphisms from  ''G''<sub>1</sub>/''Z''(''G''<sub>1</sub>) to ''G''<sub>2</sub>/''Z''(''G''<sub>2</sub>) and from ''G''<sub>1</sub>{{prime}} to ''G''<sub>2</sub>{{prime}} commuting with the commutator map.

==Examples==
All [[Abelian group]]s are isoclinic since they are equal to their centers and their commutator subgroups are always the identity subgroup.  Indeed, a group is isoclinic to an abelian group if and only if it is itself abelian, and ''G'' is isoclinic with ''G''×''A'' if and only if ''A'' is abelian.  The [[dihedral group|dihedral]], [[quasidihedral group|quasidihedral]], and [[quaternion group]]s of order 2<sup>''n''</sup> are isoclinic for ''n''≥3, {{harvtxt|Berkovich|2008|p=285}} in more detail.

Isoclinism divides ''p''-groups into families, and the smallest members of each family are called '''stem groups'''.  A group is a stem group if and only if Z(''G'') ≤ [''G'',''G''], that is, if and only if every element of the center of the group is contained in the [[derived subgroup]] (also called the commutator subgroup), {{harvtxt|Berkovich|2008|p=287}}.  Some enumeration results on isoclinism families are given in {{harvtxt|Blackburn|Neumann|Venkataraman|2007|p=226}}.

Isoclinism is used in theory of [[projective representation]]s of [[finite group]]s, as all [[Schur cover]]ing groups of a group are isoclinic, a fact already hinted at by Hall according to {{harvtxt|Suzuki|1982|p=256}}.  This is used in describing the character tables of the [[finite simple group]]s {{harv|Conway|Curtis|Norton|Parker|1985|p=xxiii|loc=Ch. 6.7}}.
